title: Everything is binary
body: Computers store everything as bits, 0 or 1, because a transistor is easiest to use as an on/off switch. 8 bits make a byte with 256 possible values. Text, photos, music and apps are all just long patterns of bits with agreed meanings.

title: Moore's law
body: In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed the number of transistors on a chip was doubling regularly; he later settled on about every two years. That steady doubling drove 50 years of cheaper, faster computers. It has slowed as transistors approach the size of a few atoms.

title: Billions of switches in your pocket
body: A modern flagship phone processor contains around 15 to 20 billion transistors, each a tiny switch only a few tens of atoms across in places. The first commercial microprocessor, Intel's 4004 from 1971, had about 2,300.

title: RAM versus storage
body: RAM is the fast working memory where running apps live; it forgets everything when power goes off. Storage (flash or SSD) is slower but keeps data. A phone with little RAM closes background apps often; one with little storage runs out of room for photos.

title: What an operating system does
body: The operating system (Android, iOS, Windows, Linux) shares the hardware between apps. It schedules which program uses the CPU, gives each app its own protected memory, manages files, and controls access to the camera, network and sensors through permissions.

title: Compilers and interpreters
body: CPUs only run machine code. A compiler translates a whole program (C, Rust, Dart) into machine code before it runs, which makes it fast. An interpreter translates and runs code line by line (classic Python), which is flexible but slower. Many languages mix both with just-in-time compilation.

title: Big-O notation
body: Big-O describes how an algorithm's work grows with input size n. O(1) is constant, O(log n) grows very slowly, O(n) grows in step, O(n²) explodes: ten times more data means a hundred times more work. Choosing a better algorithm often beats buying a faster computer.

title: Binary search
body: To find a name in a sorted list, check the middle, then throw away the half it cannot be in, and repeat. Each step halves the list, so a million sorted items need at most about 20 checks. That is O(log n), versus up to a million checks looking one by one.

title: IPv4 ran out, so IPv6 arrived
body: Every device online needs an IP address. IPv4 uses 32 bits, about 4.3 billion addresses, which ran out as phones spread. IPv6 uses 128 bits, enough for about 3.4 × 10^38 addresses. Meanwhile routers share one public IPv4 address between many devices using NAT.

title: DNS: the internet's phone book
body: Computers route traffic by IP address, but people remember names. The Domain Name System turns a name like wikipedia.org into an IP address, using a worldwide hierarchy of servers and caching answers so repeat lookups are fast. If DNS fails, sites look 'down' even when they are not.

title: What the padlock means
body: HTTPS encrypts traffic between your browser and the site, and a certificate proves you are talking to the real domain. It stops people on the same Wi-Fi reading or changing your data. It does not prove the site is honest: scam sites can have padlocks too.

title: Public-key cryptography
body: Each person has a key pair. Anything locked with your public key can only be unlocked with your private key, so strangers can send you secrets without meeting first. Reversed, it makes digital signatures: only your private key can produce a signature your public key verifies.

title: Why sites store password hashes
body: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint that cannot be reversed. Good sites store a salted, slow hash of your password, not the password. If the database leaks, attackers must guess passwords one by one, which is why long unique passwords matter.

title: Phishing
body: Phishing tricks you into giving away passwords, codes or money with a message that looks official: a bank, a delivery, a mobile money 'reversal'. Warning signs: urgency, odd links, requests for PINs or one-time codes. Real banks and mobile money providers never ask for your PIN.

title: Two-factor authentication
body: 2FA asks for something you know (password) plus something you have (a code from an app or a security key). A stolen password alone is then not enough. Authenticator apps are safer than SMS codes, because SIM-swap fraud can redirect your texts.

title: Machine learning in one idea
body: Instead of writing rules by hand, you show a model many examples and let it adjust its internal numbers until its answers match. Spam filters, face unlock, crop disease detection and speech recognition all learn patterns from data rather than following hand-written rules.

title: How large language models work
body: A large language model is a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token (a word piece). Doing that well forces it to learn grammar, facts and reasoning patterns. It can still state false things confidently, so check important answers.

title: Why GPUs power AI
body: A CPU has a few powerful cores; a GPU has thousands of simpler ones built to do the same maths on lots of numbers at once. Training neural networks is mostly multiplying huge matrices, exactly the parallel work GPUs were designed for when drawing game graphics.

title: Cloud computing
body: The cloud is other people's computers in data centres, rented by the hour. Startups can launch without buying servers and scale up when users arrive. The trade-offs: ongoing costs, dependence on a provider, and needing a good internet connection.

title: The internet runs under the sea
body: Almost all data travelling between continents goes through fibre-optic cables on the ocean floor, not satellites. Hundreds of these cables link the world, and damage to a few, as happened off West Africa in 2024, can slow internet access across many countries.

title: Mobile money changed Africa
body: Kenya's M-Pesa, launched in 2007, let people send money by SMS with no bank account. Zimbabwe's EcoCash followed in 2011. Mobile money spread fastest in Africa because phones reached people long before bank branches did.

title: Open-source software
body: Open-source code can be read, changed and shared by anyone. Linux runs most web servers and sits at the heart of Android. Companies use and contribute to open source because shared foundations are cheaper and better tested than everyone building their own.

title: Git and version control
body: Git, created by Linus Torvalds in 2005, records every change to a project's files. You can see who changed what, undo mistakes, and let many people work in parallel on branches, then merge. Almost all professional software is built this way.

title: APIs: how apps talk
body: An API is a published set of requests one program can make to another. A weather app asks a weather service's API for today's forecast; a shop checkout calls a payment API. APIs let companies build on each other without sharing their internal code.

title: Latency versus bandwidth
body: Bandwidth is how much data per second a link carries (a wide pipe). Latency is how long one message takes to arrive (a long pipe). Streaming video needs bandwidth; video calls and online games need low latency. Satellites in high orbit add big delays.

title: Quantum computers
body: Quantum computers use qubits, which can be in combinations of 0 and 1 and become entangled. They are not faster at everything, but some problems, such as simulating molecules or factoring big numbers with Shor's algorithm, could become practical. That second one threatens today's RSA encryption.

title: Who makes the world's chips
body: Designing a chip and making it are different businesses. Apple, Nvidia and Qualcomm design chips; Taiwan's TSMC manufactures most of the world's most advanced ones. A modern chip factory costs over 20 billion US dollars, which is why so few companies can build them.

title: Bits and bytes
body: Computing check.
statement: A byte is made of 8 bits
explanation: A byte is 8 bits, giving 2^8 = 256 possible values, enough for one character of basic text.

title: Reading binary
body: Number systems check.

title: Reading hexadecimal
body: Number systems check.
statement: FF in hexadecimal equals 255 in decimal
explanation: F is 15, so FF = 15×16 + 15 = 255, the largest value one byte can hold.

title: Wi-Fi and the internet
body: Networking check.
statement: Wi-Fi and the internet are the same thing
correct_answer: Wi-Fi is only the local wireless link
explanation: Wi-Fi connects your device to a nearby router. The router then connects to the internet through your provider.

title: Speed of binary search
body: Algorithms check.
statement: Binary search on a sorted list takes O(n) steps
explanation: Each step halves the list, so the number of steps grows with log n, not n.

title: Incognito mode
body: Privacy check.
statement: Incognito mode hides your browsing from your internet provider
correct_answer: It only stops your own device keeping history
explanation: Private browsing does not save history or cookies on your device. Your provider, school or employer can still see which sites you reach.
